controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Gaia DR3 spectrum color, dimmed and reddened toward the limb by the model laws of Claret, Hauschildt & Witte (2012), one band per color channel. The disc and its radial profile are unresolved; no rotation axis is measured.
controls.notes: No image of this photosphere exists: at 12.47 parsecs its disc is about 0.09 milliarcseconds across. The color is its measured spectrum through the CIE 1931 observer; below about 450 nm the star is too faint for Gaia to measure and those samples are read as no emission. Its limb plate uses the quadratic laws Claret, Hauschildt & Witte (2012) compute from PHOENIX model atmospheres at 2,566 K and log g 5.2396: the R band for the red channel, V for green and B for blue. Blue darkens most, so the edge is redder than the centre; it is a model, not a resolved measurement.

controls.label: Habitable zone
controls.notes: The star in the color of its spectrum, with its habitable zone drawn as a green band in the plane of its planets' orbits. The band is a calculation, not an observation: the distances at which a planet of Earth's mass with a carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface, by the model of Kopparapu et al. (2013, 2014), as the Habitable Zone Gallery (Kane & Gelino 2012) calculates them from the star's temperature and luminosity. The darker band is the conservative zone, 0.0246 to 0.0499 au, between the runaway greenhouse and maximum greenhouse limits; the lighter strips extend it to the optimistic zone, 0.0194 to 0.0527 au, between the recent Venus and early Mars limits. Planets e, f and g orbit in the conservative zone and d in the optimistic strip inside it. A planet in the zone is not known to be habitable, and the star is 34 K cooler than the coolest star the model was fitted to.

controls.label: Stellar wind
controls.notes: The star in the color of its spectrum, with a model of its wind drawn in the plane of its planets' orbits. The wind is the gas the star blows off; no telescope has seen TRAPPIST-1's. This is the simulation of Garraffo et al. (2017), read from the paper's Figure 3. The colors are the wind's total pressure, magnetic plus dynamic: yellow where it is highest, near the star, through orange and purple to dark blue where it is lowest. The dashed white line is the Alfvén surface: inside it the star's magnetic field still holds the wind, and outside it the wind has broken free. On the figure, planets c to g cross the line four times each orbit, b touches it twice and h stays outside. The model gives wind speeds up to about 1,400 km/s and pressures at the orbits a thousand to a million times the solar wind's at Earth. It uses the magnetic map of another star, GJ 3622, scaled to TRAPPIST-1's measured mean field of 600 G. The pattern turns with the star every 3.3 days, so the picture holds one moment; the figure prints no scale, so the colors show where the pressure is higher, not by how much.

controls.label: Tidal heating
controls.notes: The star in the color of its spectrum, with each planet's orbit line in the color of the heat tides raise inside the planet: plain gray for none, through amber to red for the most. A planet on a slightly oval orbit is pulled harder by its star when it is nearer and less when it is farther; the flexing warms its rock. The values are the model of Barr, Dobos & Kiss (2018), their Table 3, in watts per square metre of the planet's surface: b 2.68, c 1.32, d 0.16, e 0.18, f 0.14, g 0 and h 0. By the paper's own comparison Io, Jupiter's volcanic moon, has about 1 to 2. The uncertainties are large: b's value stands between 0.87 and 4.01. The model rests on the masses and orbit shapes published in 2017, and later papers give other values for some planets. No heat from any of these planets has been measured.
